original_question: Given points a_1, ..., a_m in a Euclidean space X, can one write an explicit and neat formula or characterization for the unique minimizer of min_{x in X} max_{i in {1, ..., m}} ||a_i - x||, that is, for the center of the smallest Euclidean sphere containing all the points? More generally, what analogous description is available when X is an arbitrary normed or metric space, or when the maximum over the m distances is replaced by an arbitrary norm on R^m?
target_in_paper: Section 7, "Minimal Distance Problem" (the open problem proposed by Alex Kruger), especially equation (2) and the surrounding discussion of explicit representations. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper. It reproduces the exact Euclidean minimax problem from Section 7, correctly identifies the Euclidean minimizer as the center of the minimal enclosing sphere, and also captures the two extensions explicitly mentioned there: allowing X to be an arbitrary normed linear or metric space, and replacing the maximum by an arbitrary norm on R^m. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
missing_details: The paper states the problem for a finite set of points a_1, ..., a_m in a Euclidean space X; the finiteness of the index set should be stated explicitly. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

The paper's emphasis is not on algorithms or numerical methods, but on whether the solution can be written in a neat explicit form; that exclusion should be stated to match the paper's intent. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
In the metric-space version, the norm of a_i - x is to be replaced by the distance d(a_i, x). ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

To make the R^m-generalization stand-alone, one should say explicitly that the arbitrary norm on R^m is applied to the m-tuple of distances from x to the given points; this is the natural reading of the paper's sentence that the maximum can be replaced by an arbitrary norm in R^m. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

Uniqueness is asserted in the paper only for the Euclidean formulation; the paper does not state a corresponding uniqueness claim for the broader normed or metric formulations. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

The paper gives the one-dimensional example x = (max_i a_i + min_i a_i)/2 in R, which helps specify the kind of explicit representation being sought. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
refined_question: Let a_1, ..., a_m be a finite set of points in a Euclidean space X. Determine whether the solution of min_{x in X} max_{1<=i<=m} ||a_i - x|| can be represented in a neat explicit form, rather than merely computed numerically; equivalently, describe explicitly the unique point x that is the center of the minimal Euclidean sphere containing {a_1, ..., a_m}. More generally, for X a normed linear space or even a metric space (with ||a_i - x|| replaced by d(a_i, x) in the metric case), and with the objective max_{1<=i<=m} d(a_i, x) replaced by an arbitrary norm on R^m applied to the vector of distances (d(a_1, x), ..., d(a_m, x)), determine when such a solution admits an explicit representation. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: In the Euclidean case, this is equivalently the problem of finding the center of the minimal Euclidean sphere containing all the points a_1, ..., a_m. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
justification: Section 1 says that Section 7 asks about representations for a minimal distance problem. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf)) Section 7 then states exactly the minimax problem in your draft, says that its Euclidean solution is unique and is the center of the minimal enclosing Euclidean sphere, and immediately broadens the discussion to arbitrary normed linear spaces, metric spaces, and arbitrary norms on R^m. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf)) The same paragraph also clarifies that the point of the open problem is explicit representation rather than numerical solution and gives the one-dimensional midpoint formula as the model example. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf)) For that reason, the refined question keeps your formulation essentially intact, but makes explicit the finite-point hypothesis, the metric-space replacement of the norm by a distance, the intended meaning of the R^m-norm generalization, and the paper's focus on explicit representability.
